rationale: T2P217 reports black tea among the most consumed beverages in a cross-sectional adult survey. It provides no gait or Parkinson outcome.
T1P123 used a blueberry polyphenol extract in a rat metabolic model. T4P235 reports food-matched IgG markers, without a clinical challenge. Neither gives a raw-blueberry constipation comparison.
T2P44 and T2P112 record broccoli in diet inventories and assess macular pigment or estimated indole intake. T4P235 reports a food marker with no clinical challenge. None measures broccoli and falls.
T2P112 lists cauliflower as a cruciferous source in 24-hour food recalls. It gives no verified roast preparation or anxiety observation.
T2P19 reports use of chicken label information. T2P4 and T2P79 describe poultry within model menus or a combined dietary group. They do not establish poached chicken intake and fatigue.

T2P217 and T2P75 report beverage consumption. T2P126 models adiposity, T1P147 is a dysbiosis analysis, and T4P95 and T4P192 use coffee as a covariate or mealtime option. None estimates Parkinson fatigue.

T1P123 gives a cranberry polyphenol extract versus saline in the metabolic-syndrome model. Triglycerides were lower; the animal count and route description differ within the poster. There is no dried cranberry depression result.
The matched words refer to chronology and calendars. Neither the body nor alternate-name search reveals an edible date-palm exposure.

T2P44 and T2P53 report eggs in diet recalls or intake surveys; T2P74 and T2P79 have eggs in combined food groups. T2P19 and T2P36 concern labels and nutrition knowledge. None assigned poached eggs or measured Parkinson gait and falls.

T1P44 measures brown adipose outcomes after isolated resveratrol. This is a grape-associated constituent with unverified source and no anxiety measure. T4P206 describes a visual resemblance rather than a grape exposure.
T4P189 combines oral green tea and extracts in a pooled weight and body-composition analysis. The reported intervals span zero, and no fatigue assessment is supplied.
T2P112 records kale among sources in the dietary recall; the outcome is estimated indole intake, without a falls or roasted-kale comparison.
T2P217 reports kefir in adult beverage intakes and an inconclusive sex difference. Product composition and falls were not evaluated.

T1P104 studies a chemically structured blend containing olive oil, T1P127 studies two olive-oil fat levels in mouse diets, and T4P152 discusses a leaf product. None gives a matching culinary-oil symptom outcome.
T2P44 includes orange juice in carotenoid intake and T4P235 reports an IgG marker for pooled citrus. T3P131 uses orange as a color. No study measured raw-orange falls or constipation.
The only parsley reference, T2P44, says none of the relevant subgroup consumed it. No parsley exposure or ingredient-specific outcome contributes to the comparison.

T1P158 tests potato-derived fibers in buns and measures appetite and fecal outputs. Other posters report potatoes in combined diets, purchases and snack categories, without roasted potato or insomnia findings.

T4P140 compares supplemental safflower oil with fish oil in an abdominal-obesity crossover. The trial registration and later reports identify linked lipid and biomarker outcomes without swallow, anxiety or fall results.
T4P199 combines fish-oil concentrate and a salmon meal in a small six-month before-and-after study. It measures blood biomarkers without isolated poached-salmon effects or anxiety.

T1P52 and T1P75 compare a high-oleic sunflower-oil diet at 40% of the mixture with palm oil and standard chow in mice. The outcomes are adipose gene expression and Y-maze alternation, with no verified cold-pressed preparation or Parkinson phenotype.
T2P151 tests curcumin with a weight-loss diet in PCOS, while T3P37 uses turmeric in a child bread-preference study. These preparations and populations do not answer the Parkinson claims.
T2P44 reports some students got carotenoids from foods including zucchini. Grill preparation and executive function were not assessed.
